title: The Baztán Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Baztanes
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.

spans.t: The Camino Baztanés is a small road through a very green country. It leaves Bayonne, in the French Basque Country, climbs over the western end of the Pyrenees by two passes, runs down the Baztán valley of Navarre, and ends in Pamplona, where it meets the Camino Francés. (The app's catalogue spells the name
Baztanes
, without the accent. Spanish sources write
Baztanés
, and so does this book.) Visit Navarra, the region's official tourism website, divides it into six walking days that add up to ~109 km.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know what each of the six days asks of you, what to check before you set out, and where the road leads when it ends.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order, then the days, and the chapter on other ways to split them: the sources do not agree on how many days this road has. If you are on the road tonight, go to your stage, and read "Body, weather and safety" before Day 3 and again before Day 5. If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.

It is also not a Compostela book. The Compostela, the certificate of the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago, belongs to a walk that arrives at the cathedral of Santiago. This road ends in Pamplona, and the French Way carries on from there.
Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season (snow, mist, a muddy path), the book says
check before you go
, and means it. On a mountain road in a wet climate, that line matters.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way; each stamp is a
sello
. A
puerto
is a mountain pass (the French word is
col
). In Navarre the official pages give most place names in Basque and Spanish together, such as Urdazubi/Urdax and Amaiur/Maya. The glossary at the end has the rest.
Pack something waterproof, start the long days early, and be kind to your feet.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes
The Camino Baztanés (in French
la voie du Baztan

) runs from Bayonne to Pamplona. The app's catalogue gives it those two ends, in France and Spain, and no length. The public sources do. Visit Navarra's blog splits the road into six stages totalling ~109 km, and the Camino pages of a Spanish consumer guide, Eroski Consumer, give the same six stages and the same total. Both put ~32 of those kilometres in the French Basque Country and ~77 in Navarre.

The road starts at the Gothic cathedral of Bayonne and follows the river Nive upstream. It climbs through the hills of Labourd, the French Basque province, to Ainhoa, and crosses the frontier at Dantxarinea, a district of the Navarrese village of Urdazubi/Urdax. Then it goes over the pass of Otsondo into the Baztán valley, follows the valley to Elizondo, climbs over the pass of Belate, and comes down the Ultzama valley to the edge of Pamplona. At the medieval bridge of the Trinity, in the village of Arre, it meets the Camino Francés. The last ~5 km, by Villava and Burlada, are on the French Way.

Bayonne is a crossroads. Its tourist office says it lies where two ways meet, the Camino del Norte and the Voie de Soulac, and that you can join the Camino Francés at Pamplona by continuing on the Baztán road from there. That is the road's place: a quiet way in to the Francés, or a week's walk in its own right.
What kind of road it is

The French association of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques, the Amis du chemin de St-Jacques, calls it a little-known road through the green landscapes of the northern Basque Country and the equally green valleys of Navarre, and says it crosses the Pyrenees by the lowest pass, Belate. Visit Navarra says that pass is considerably lower than the entrances of the French and Aragonese Ways. Sources give its height differently: ~847 m (the French association, and French Wikipedia), about 900 m (the association's own description of the day), ~938 m (Visit Navarra's blog). Otsondo is ~670 m, says French Wikipedia. Whatever the height, the climbs to both are real.

The app's route notes describe the road as hilly, with forest paths, and say rain is common; they call it a small route where you need to plan your stops. Expect woods, field gates, stone farmhouses, a few small towns and long stretches with none.
A road with a long memory

Visit Navarra calls it one of the oldest paths in Navarre. In the Middle Ages, its blog says, armies, merchants and kings used it to cross the Pyrenees, and from the ninth century European pilgrims did too, especially people from Aquitaine and Brittany. The proof, it says, is the pilgrims' hospitals and monasteries of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, known from their remains and from deeds of donation. It names the monasteries of Urdazubi/Urdax and Belate. A 1964 study by Padre Germán de Pamplona argued that the Bayonne to Pamplona road by Belate was far busier than people thought, and Eroski Consumer says the study has guided the road's recovery.

The recovery is recent. Eroski says the Association of Friends of the Camino de Santiago in Urdax-Baztán began in 2000 to recover the road, and a pilgrim-hostel directory, Albergues del Camino, says it was close to lost in places and that volunteers cleared paths with brushcutters. According to both, the little chapel of Santiago at Belate was reopened in 2016. The directory also reports the association's own account that documents about the road go back to the twelfth century. Treat that as a claim, not a proof.
When the sources disagree

Lengths differ from source to source, and so do the stages. This book follows Visit Navarra's six stages, which Eroski repeats. The French association's own topo offers five stages totalling ~108 km, and the directory counts six stages from Bayonne to Arre, ~103 km. Visit Navarra's own route page shows ~86 km for the part from Urdazubi/Urdax to Arre, which does not match its blog's ~77 km in Navarre; this book uses the blog's figures. Each day's heading gives a rounded length, and the chapter on other ways to split the road shows the alternatives. Treat every figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
How hard is it?

The app's catalogue rates the Camino Baztanés 3 on a scale of 1 to 5. That is the rating it gives the Camino Francés, one less than the Primitivo and one more than the Camino Inglés. It is a middle rating for a short road, and it hides an uneven week.
Visit Navarra's official page calls the road gentle and beautiful. The detailed stage descriptions show where the effort is. Day 2 has a hilly first ~13.5 km that its sources call
rompepiernas

, "leg-breakers". Day 3 begins with the climb to Otsondo. Day 5 crosses Belate, which Eroski Consumer calls the queen stage and measures at more than ~600 m of accumulated climbing between Almandoz and the pass. Eroski rates Days 1, 4 and 6 as easy or nearly so, though Day 6 is the longest, at ~25 km. The distances are small, ~109 km in six days, but this is a mountain road in a wet country, and it asks for a proper start.
Who it suits

items.t: Walkers who want a quiet green week.
Visit Navarra says the road is less crowded than the French Way, and that it keeps away from road traffic.
Walkers who want to reach the Francés from the north.
Bayonne's tourist office presents the road as the way to join the French Way at Pamplona.
Walkers coming off the coastal road.
The French association says the road is recommended to those who start in Bayonne or who arrive on foot from the coastal route.
A first Camino, with care.
The days are short, but the first marks on the French side are small, and beds can be scarce in high season. Read the chapters on before you go and on safety.

spans.t: Who might choose something else

items.t: Anyone who wants a Compostela from this walk.
The road ends ~712 km short of Santiago, so it is the first part of a longer walk, not a route to the cathedral. The chapter on arriving explains.
Anyone who wants company and services at every turn.
Visit Navarra says the French Way is better waymarked and has more services than this road. Several stage ends are small villages.
Anyone who cannot cope with a wet day.
Rain is common here. It is a reason to carry good waterproofs, not a reason to stay at home, but it may be a reason to choose a drier month.
Anyone who needs a guaranteed bed each night.
Eroski says beds may be scarce in high season, and a pilgrim-hostel directory says some small hostels work by prior notice. A planner who must know where the night will be will want to book.

spans.t: How it compares

Do not expect the busy road of the Francés. Visit Navarra says that its well-known sister is better signed and better served, and that this road offers big green landscapes and, above all, fewer crowds. It adds that some people link the road with the Camino Primitivo because it keeps off the traffic. The French Way is the great road. This is a small way into it, and on the last day, where the two meet, you may see other pilgrims for the first time in days.

If two days of ~20 km running, with your loaded pack, sound like too much, plan the shorter splits in the chapter on other ways to cut the road, and take a rest day in Elizondo, the main town on the way.
The weather, in patterns

This road is green because it is wet. Meteo Navarra, the weather and climate service of the regional government, describes the valleys of northern Navarre as having an oceanic climate, with abundant rain, fog and drizzle, and calls this the rainiest part of Navarre. Its page on that zone uses Doneztebe/Santesteban, a town in the same part of Navarre, as its example, so the figures below are the page's, for the zone, not for one village on your route. No weather table for the French half was read for this book; for that, ask Météo-France, the national weather service.

items.t: Spring.
Changeable and rainy. Average daytime highs rise from ~16 °C in March to ~21 °C in May in the valleys, with ~260 to ~570 mm of rain over the three months.
Summer.

Mild: in July and August, the daily lows and highs average between ~11 and ~26 °C. It is the least rainy season, and rain is still frequent: ~120 to ~360 mm over the three months. The page says plainly that there is no summer drought.
Autumn.
September is still summery, with an afternoon average of ~25 °C in Doneztebe/Santesteban. By November it falls to ~14.8 °C and the rain is abundant again, ~250 to ~650 mm over the season.
Winter.
The mildest winters in Navarre, the page says, with a January average of ~7.2 °C in Doneztebe/Santesteban, and wet. Higher and further inland, it adds, winters are colder.

spans.t: Over a year the zone gets between ~900 and ~2,500 mm of rain, depending on the place. The ridge of Belate and Azpirotz acts as a screen against the wet fronts from the north and north-west, and the southern valleys beyond it, among them the Ultzama, keep some of the oceanic character. Pamplona lies in a different zone. Meteo Navarra calls it sub-oceanic: drier than the valleys, with a dry season in summer and July and August maxima that average ~28 to ~30 °C.

The app's route notes suggest May to September. The pattern fits: summer is the least rainy season, though on this road no month is dry. In winter, Eroski Consumer warns that snow is easy to find at the pass of Belate.
Daylight

These are the book's own figures, calculated from a standard solar formula for Elizondo, in local clock time. They are approximate, and you should check a sun table before you plan. Navarre keeps Central European Time, with summer time from spring to autumn.

items.t: Late December: sunrise ~08:35, sunset ~17:35, about 9 hours of daylight.
Mid-November: sunset ~17:45.
Mid-April: sunset ~20:45.
Mid-May: sunset ~21:20.
Late June: sunrise ~06:25, sunset ~21:50, about 15 hours of daylight.
Late September: sunset ~20:10.
Mid-October: sunset ~19:25.

spans.t: From late autumn to early spring, plan for ~9 to ~10 hours of light, start at first light, and carry a head torch. The two hard days, over Otsondo and over Belate, are the ones not to start late.
Crowds and quiet

No count of pilgrims on this road was found in a source that could be checked: the Pilgrim's Office's statistics page is built by script and could not be read. Visit Navarra's blog says the road is far less popular than the French Way.
Pamplona is the exception, in July. Wikipedia says the San Fermín festival runs from noon on 6 July to midnight on 14 July, and the city fills. If you plan to arrive then, book your bed well ahead.
Check before you go

Rain, mist, a path closed after a storm, snow at the pass: these change from year to year and from day to day. Meteo Navarra publishes forecasts for Navarre, and Visit Navarra's Camino page links to one made for the Camino de Santiago. Check Visit Navarra's pages and the French association's website for notices, look at the forecast the evening before and again at breakfast, and ask locally on the way.
Your credencial
The
credencial
is the pilgrim's passport: a folded card with boxes for the stamps, or
sellos

, that you collect on the way. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says the stamps are normally collected where pilgrims sleep, but can also be had in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, town halls and other places. It also says where an official card comes from: parish churches, associations of friends of the Way, pilgrim hostels, confraternities and other authorised institutions, in Spain and abroad. The Confraternity of St James in Britain, for example, says its pilgrim credencial is accredited by Santiago Cathedral.

The simplest plan is to bring a card from home. If you would rather get one on the road, an Eroski Consumer note, of uncertain date, says that credencials and stamps could be had at Bayonne's cathedral, and the association of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques lists a pilgrims' refuge in Bayonne among its activities. None of this is a promise, so ask. On this road the card is your key to the pilgrims' hostels.
Getting there, and getting back

Visit Navarra's blog describes two usual ways to begin. Most people who start in Navarre, it says, travel to Pamplona, take a bus to Elizondo and then a taxi to Urdazubi/Urdax. Others begin in Bayonne, reached by bus from San Sebastián. Starting at Urdax skips the French half, ~36 km, and begins with Day 3.

This book names no timetables, because they change, and none of the pages read for it gives a current timetable for either end of this road. Look before you leave home, ask at your hostel or the tourist office, and do not plan a train or a flight for the afternoon of your last walking day.
Training and packing

The Xunta de Galicia, the regional government of Galicia, publishes general advice for pilgrims, and it applies here. Do not set off untrained. Take long walks in the weeks before you go, lengthen them gradually, and plan stages that fit your fitness. With a longest day of ~25 km and two long climbs, a practice walk of ~20 km with your loaded pack is a fair test.

Keep the pack light. The Xunta says a correctly packed rucksack should not exceed 10 kg, with padded straps, and that a waterproof garment belongs in the pack regardless of the time of year. On a wet mountain road, that advice is the heart of the list:

items.t: Rain gear that works.
A jacket, something for your legs or a poncho that also covers your pack, and a bag or liner so your dry clothes stay dry.
A warm layer
for the passes, where the sources speak of mist.
Shoes with grip.

The Xunta says footwear must be broken in, with hard soles for rough ground, and that new stiff shoes will hurt you. It recommends seamless socks, and drying your feet thoroughly, because damp feet invite fungus.
A head torch
, for the short days of the year.
A map you can use without signal.

The waymarks on the French side are small, and a pilgrim-hostel directory advises downloading the track before the day of Belate. The app's catalogue lists this road with its two ends and no stage-by-stage data, so carry a track from another source and make sure it works offline.

spans.t: Money, papers and language

The Xunta advises carrying your documents and cards rather than a lot of cash. Several stage ends are small villages, so keep a little cash for places that do not take cards. The Policía Foral, the regional police of Navarre, asks pilgrims to keep their passport or national identity card in a safe place. You are crossing an international frontier on foot, so carry yours.

The first two days are in France, and French helps there. After the frontier it is Spanish, and the official pages of Navarre give place names in Basque and Spanish together, such as Urdazubi/Urdax, Amaiur/Maya and Doneztebe/Santesteban. A few polite words in each language,
bonjour
merci
buenos días
gracias
, go a long way.
The character of these days

Two days in the French Basque Country: a river and a ridge. The first is flat and easy. The second is hilly and wooded, and it ends in Spain. The lengths in this book follow Visit Navarra's blog, which Eroski Consumer repeats; the chapter on other ways to split the road shows the alternatives.
These are the two days to watch the waymarks. The French association says the road is marked
voie du Baztan

all the way to the frontier, and that beyond it you follow the Spanish yellow arrows. Eroski says the French marks are small, and that you must pay more attention to the Camino here than you will later.
Day 1: Bayonne to Ustaritz (~14 km)

Visit Navarra's blog says this stage has no difficulty and puts it at about three hours. It begins in front of Bayonne's Gothic cathedral, which the city's tourist office says UNESCO listed in 1998 among the monuments of the
Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France
. The French association also starts you from its pilgrims' refuge in the city. Either way you go down to the river Nive and keep it beside you.
Almost the whole day is the Nive's towpath, the
chemin de halage

, which Eroski explains was the path from which mules pulled the merchants' barges. It runs flat between orchards, fields and riverside trees, under a motorway and a railway bridge. The day ends at Ustaritz, where Eroski mentions the church of St Vincent, of the nineteenth century.

Use the easy day to learn what the Camino's mark looks like, because tomorrow asks more of you. For a longer first day, Eroski says the stage can be stretched to Souraïde or Espelette, ~25 km from Bayonne, which is also the French association's first stage.
Day 2: Ustaritz to Urdazubi/Urdax (~21 km)
Visit Navarra's blog gives this day about five and a half hours, and says the first ~13.5 km are the leg-breakers,
rompepiernas
. After that it is gentler. The Spanish original of Eroski's page says the same: a day of two halves.

You leave Ustaritz by the old town hall square and climb through oak and chestnut woods, crossing small streams, and then follow gravel tracks between meadows. Eroski points to two places in the first ~4 km where it says many pilgrims lose the way, and advises following only the marks of the
voie du Baztan
, since other yellow marks lead to local routes. Espelette, famous for its pepper, is about a kilometre off the way, says Eroski.

Souraïde, ~10 km into the day, has a church dedicated to St James, says the French association. Above the village the way climbs to the Col de Pinodieta, where Eroski warns that it crosses another Camino, the one from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Irun. Cross the road and carry straight on.
Then comes the descent to Ainhoa. The Pyrénées-Atlantiques tourism site, Tourisme 64, says Ainhoa is a
bastide-rue

, a village laid out along one broad street, built in the twelfth century to welcome pilgrims on the voie du Baztan; its church of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption is of the thirteenth century and has tiers of galleries. The commune's own page says the village straddles the frontier with Spain, and that the pilgrims' road passes through it.

From Ainhoa small roads and low rises lead to the frontier, ~18 km into the day. On the French side the last district is Dantxaria, which belongs to Ainhoa; on the Spanish side it is Dantxarinea, a district of Urdazubi/Urdax. Eroski says Dantxarinea has lived on border trade for generations, and that you pass the old customs buildings and a small stream, the Lapitxuri, as you enter Spain. Then the yellow arrows begin, and a path beside the Ugarana river leads on to Urdazubi/Urdax.

Visit Navarra's blog says the monastery here had a pilgrims' hospital, and its route page says the caves of Urdazubi/Urdax, carved by the river Urtxuma and about 14,000 years old, can be visited on a guided tour. Ask locally when. Tomorrow starts with a climb.
Care.

At Dantxarinea the way runs beside a national road, the N-121-B, and a little later it leaves the road at a Jacobean milestone, says Eroski. Watch for the turn, and watch the traffic. On this day the marks are small, so check your track at each junction in the first hour.

chapters.title: The Baztán valley: Urdax to Berroeta

spans.t: The character of these days

Two days through the heart of the valley that gives the road its name. Visit Navarra describes it as one of the most idyllic of the Atlantic Pyrenean valleys of Navarre, a country of soft green hills, stone farmhouses with pinkish stonework, and cattle in the meadows. The first day begins with a climb and ends in the valley's main town. The second is short and quiet, a day to prepare for Belate.
Day 3: Urdazubi/Urdax to Elizondo (~19 km)

Visit Navarra's blog puts this stage at ~18.8 km and about four and a half hours, and tells you to take the pass of Otsondo, at the start of the day, very calmly. The climb begins as soon as you leave the village. A pilgrim-hostel directory counts ~450 m of climbing in the first stretch, and French Wikipedia puts the pass at ~670 m. Eroski Consumer describes strong gradients on a rough track at first, then a forest track, in woods that it says are thick and easily wrapped in mist, and the French association says the same of Otsondo. Keep your track open.

The descent brings you into the valley and to Amaiur/Maya, ~10 km into the day. Visit Navarra tells its story. Navarre lost the independence of its kingdom in 1512, and troops loyal to the Navarrese crown held the castle of Amaiur until they were defeated in 1522: the last redoubt of resistance. Only ruins remain on the hill of Gaztelu, with a monolith put up in their memory, and the village has a museum about the castle. The village itself is a single street of farmhouses of every local style, entered through a porticoed arch, with a medieval church of the Assumption and a restored mill that has ground maize since the eighteenth century.

After Amaiur the way follows an old road above the valley. The directory says there are two ways out of the village, one by Urrasun and one by Bozate, and that they rejoin at Arizkun. Eroski describes the one by Urrasun, past a hermitage of Santiago restored in 2007 and 2008. Visit Navarra says Bozate is the quarter of Arizkun where the
agotes
lived, a people who suffered exclusion and about whom much has been speculated. Beyond Arizkun the path runs near the river, through Elbete, and then you cross into Elizondo.

Elizondo is the main town of the valley. Visit Navarra says its mansions and palaces reflect the wealth that emigrants to America brought home, and names the baroque palace of Arizkunenea, of 1730, and the baroque church of Santiago. Its blog says the road stops in Elizondo, where you can reach more services if you need them, and its route page praises the town's chocolate with hazelnuts.
Day 4: Elizondo to Berroeta (~10 km)

The shortest day of the road. Visit Navarra's blog calls it a simple stage of ~9.7 km, about two and a quarter hours, and Eroski says there are no serious difficulties, only a short climb to Zigaurre.

You leave Elizondo past the town hall, cross the river and follow it, and pass the villages of Lekaroz and Irurita. Visit Navarra says Irurita is the second most populous village of the valley, with fine civil architecture. Then the way rises to Zigaurre and its chapel of San Andrés, with a viewpoint over the valley a little off the path, and comes to Ziga. Visit Navarra says its parish church of St Lawrence is surprisingly big for so small a village, and Eroski and the French association say the locals call it the cathedral. Then Aniz, and Berroeta.
Use the short day well: wash your clothes, rest your feet, and read the weather for Belate. The chapter on other ways to split the road shows how some walkers go further today, to shorten tomorrow.

chapters.title: Belate and the road to Pamplona

spans.t: The character of these days

One mountain day and one long walk down. The first crosses the ridge of Belate from the Baztán valley into the Ultzama, the hardest ground of the whole road. The second follows rivers and valleys to the edge of Pamplona and ends where you meet the French Way. Read "Body, weather and safety" before Day 5.
Day 5: Berroeta to Olagüe (~20 km)

This is the hard day, and Eroski Consumer and a pilgrim-hostel directory both say so. Visit Navarra's blog gives ~20.4 km, about five hours, with two thirds of the stage through woods and mid-mountain country. Eroski calls it the queen stage and counts more than ~600 m of accumulated climbing between Almandoz and the pass. The directory says the weather weighs more here than on any other day: rain, mud or fog can slow you a good deal.

You go down from Berroeta to Almandoz, ~2 km away, and then climb for a long time, first through chestnut woods. Eroski says the climb passes an inn that stands where an old hostel for wayfarers and pilgrims once did, then goes on up a steep forest path over Mount Larrondo and Mount Arluz. At the top, stone markers line the way, and close by is the hermitage of Santiago, of the twelfth century, rebuilt after a long effort and blessed in 2016, say Eroski and the directory.

Near here the way crosses the line between the Atlantic and Mediterranean river basins, says Eroski, and the pass is the boundary of the Baztán and Ultzama valleys. Below it lies the monastery of Santa María de Belate. French Wikipedia says the old hospital there received pilgrims on the Baztán road, and Visit Navarra names Belate with Urdax as the road's notable monasteries. Eroski dates the hospital to the twelfth century, and quotes a letter of 1378 from the bishop of Bayonne, reported by Padre Germán de Pamplona, saying that countless men would be lost and die in these mountains and forests, especially in winter, were it not for the food, help and guidance the hospital gave to all who passed.
Heights differ by source, as the first chapter says: ~847 m, about 900 m, ~938 m.

The forest path down to Lantz, ~15 km into the day, is the loneliest part. Eroski says the road runs close to the path as far as the monastery of Belate, so help is near on the climb. Beyond it, the path crosses the young Ultzama river and runs through beech woods where the track fades and you must watch for the yellow arrows. Lantz is on the normal route, ~4 km before Olagüe, and the directory suggests it as an earlier stop if the pass has taken longer than planned. Olagüe is the capital of the Anué valley, says Eroski, with a baroque parish church.
Care.

Start early, and decide the evening before whether the conditions are right. If you are in doubt, ask locally, and do not cross in thick mist or on snow you cannot judge. The chapter on safety says more.
Day 6: Olagüe to Pamplona (~25 km)
The last day is the longest, and a gentle one. Visit Navarra's blog calls it simple, though longer, ~25 km, about six hours, and Eroski says it has little or no difficulty.

The way crosses the small valleys of the Anué, the Odieta and the Olaibar, through Leazkue, Etulain, Burutain, Ostiz, Enderiz and Olaiz. Eroski says the path between Enderiz and Olaiz can be muddy after a little rain, and may have a fallen tree across it. It also says there is no place to eat until Sorauren, ~14 km into the day, which has a medieval bridge of four arches. Carry food and water. After Sorauren comes ~6 km along the river park of the Ultzama, then an industrial estate and the city's ring road, and then Arre.

At Arre you reach the medieval bridge of the Trinity, ~20 km from Olagüe. Here the Camino Baztanés meets the Camino Francés. On the far side of the bridge, says Eroski, is the old hospital of the Trinity, a pilgrims' hostel today, with its Romanesque basilica; Visit Navarra's page on the French Way describes the basilica at Arre as of Romanesque origin. The French Way goes straight on through Villava and Burlada to the river Arga and the old city. Eroski puts Arre ~4.6 km from the centre, and the directory ~4.9 km, so the ~25 km of the day are really ~20 km of the Baztán road and ~5 km of the French Way.
If your legs say stop, you can end the day at Arre: the directory ends its sixth stage there. Otherwise carry on to the old town, and read the chapter on arriving.

chapters.title: Other ways to split the road

spans.t: Three ways to count

The sources keep to the old stage towns, but they do not agree on how many days there are, or on how long each is. This book uses the first split below, the one Visit Navarra proposes. The French association of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques and a pilgrim-hostel directory propose the others.

items.t: Visit Navarra's six stages, Bayonne to Pamplona, ~109 km.

Bayonne to Ustaritz ~14 km. Ustaritz to Urdazubi/Urdax ~21 km. Urdazubi/Urdax to Elizondo ~19 km. Elizondo to Berroeta ~10 km. Berroeta to Olagüe ~20 km. Olagüe to Pamplona ~25 km. Eroski Consumer gives the same figures.
The French association's five stages, ~108 km.
Bayonne to Souraïde ~25 km. Souraïde to Amaiur ~21 km. Amaiur to Berroeta ~19 km. Berroeta to Olagüe ~20 km. Olagüe to Pamplona ~24 km. This plan passes through Urdax and Elizondo without stopping.
The directory's six stages, Bayonne to Arre, ~103 km.

Bayonne to Ustaritz ~14 km. Ustaritz to Urdazubi/Urdax ~22 km. Urdazubi/Urdax to Amaiur/Maya ~10 km. Amaiur/Maya to Berroeta ~18 km. Berroeta to Olagüe ~20 km. Olagüe to Arre ~20 km. This is the only plan that ends at the junction with the French Way, not in Pamplona, and it puts the climb to Otsondo on a short day.

spans.t: Where the same stage appears in two sources, the figures differ by a kilometre or two, and the sources do not say why. Treat each figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
A longer way to Urdax

The French association offers a second route from Bayonne to Urdax, by Saint-Pée-sur-Nivelle and Sare. On its figures this is ~24 km to Saint-Pée and ~19 km on to Urdax, so ~43 km against ~36 km by Ainhoa. It leaves the Nive early, passes through Sare, and shares part of its path with the long-distance walking path GR 10, with red and white marks, as far as the frontier. This book follows the way by Ainhoa, which Visit Navarra and Eroski both describe.
Making a hard day easier
You can change the day that troubles you without leaving the road.

items.t: Otsondo.

The directory ends its third stage at Amaiur/Maya, only ~10 km, so the climb comes early and the rest of the day is yours. Eroski says the opposite is possible: Day 3 can be lengthened to Berroeta, ~28 km, which joins Days 3 and 4 into one long day with the climb at the start.
Belate.

Eroski suggests going ~5 km beyond Berroeta on Day 4, to the inn on the climb, so the pass comes at the end of a shorter day. The directory points out that Lantz, ~15 km from Berroeta and ~4 km short of Olagüe, lies on the normal route and can end the day if the pass takes longer than planned. In both cases, check that there is a bed before you rely on the plan.
The last day.
Arre is ~20 km from Olagüe, and Pamplona is ~5 km further. You may want the old town as the end of your walk, or prefer to sleep at the junction.

spans.t: Rest days
With six days of walking you may not want a rest day at all. Two places suit one.
Elizondo
is the main town of the valley, with more services than the villages around it, and a day there makes sense if the weather turns before Belate: a day of waiting costs less than a mistake on the pass.
Pamplona
is a city that fills a day, and the chapter on arriving says why.
Check before you go.
Stage ends on this road are small. Ask in the app or by phone about beds and the next day's weather, and keep a second plan.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero
, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office says that hostels without subsidies are kept going within austerity, with contributions from pilgrims.

On this road the hostels are small, and they are run by different hands: Eroski Consumer and a pilgrim-hostel directory describe an association of friends of the Way, parishes and town councils. Visit Navarra's blog counts a hostel about every ~11.5 km on average in Navarre, so a bed is not on every corner. The directory says several stage ends are small villages, and that some hostels work by prior notice or by collecting a key. Eroski says beds may be scarce in high season. This book lists none of them, because they change. Use the app and the phone, and book ahead, above all for the end of a hard day.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and pack your rucksack in the hall, not in the dark by your bed.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed. Earplugs go a long way, and if you are the one who snores, apologise at breakfast.

spans.t: Bedbugs can turn up in any shared bed. Look at the seams of the mattress before you lie down, and if you are bitten tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. If you are ill or sleeping badly, take a private room.
Eating
Visit Navarra's pages name what to look for: the curd of the Ultzama (
cuajada
), grilled beef chops (
chuletones
), the set meals of the cider houses, the chocolate with hazelnuts of Elizondo, and the corn flatbreads called
talos
from the mill at Amaiur. On the French side Eroski points to the Espelette pepper, which hangs drying on the houses. In Pamplona, Visit Navarra recommends the
pinchos
, small bites served in the bars of the old town.

Eating on the road takes planning. Eroski's notes mention long stretches with nothing: the climb of Otsondo, the forest beyond Belate down to Lantz, and the first ~14 km of the last day, as far as Sorauren. They also name places that close one day a week, a Monday or a Tuesday. Those details change, so treat them as a warning, not a list. Buy food the evening before a long day, and carry enough for a whole day on Days 3, 5 and 6.
The Xunta's health advice for pilgrims is to drink about two litres of water a day, and never to go beyond fifteen kilometres without drinking. Fill your bottle whenever you can, even when it rains.
Resting
A short road is easy to treat as a sprint. Do not.
Elizondo
, the main town of the valley, has more services than the villages round it, says Visit Navarra's blog, and a day there before Belate is a sound use of a day if the weather has turned.
Pamplona
is a city to spend a day in, and the chapter on arriving says why.
On the road, listen to your body before your plan. If a pain grows instead of fading, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
Feet, and the wet

On a road where rain is common, feet are the first thing to suffer. The Xunta's advice for pilgrims is to wear shoes that are broken in, to wash and dry your socks whenever you stop, to dry your feet thoroughly after any wetting, and to see a pharmacist or a doctor for anything that worries you. Do it early. A small blister on Day 2 is a large one by Day 5.
Mist, mud and the two hard days

The two hard days are the days when the weather decides. The French association says Otsondo is easily wrapped in mist, and Eroski Consumer says the same of its woods. A pilgrim-hostel directory says that on Day 5 the weather weighs more than on any other day, and that after several days of rain or in fog the going can be much slower.

items.t: Look at the forecast the evening before, and again at breakfast,
and start early on Days 3 and 5. Both have a long climb, and both are better done with a margin of daylight.
On Day 5, know where you are.

Eroski says the road runs close to the path as far as the monastery of Belate, so help is near on the climb. From there to Lantz the path runs through forest, and Eroski calls it the loneliest part. If you cannot see the next mark, go back to the last one, and do not carry on in the hope that the cloud will lift.
In winter, snow.

Eroski says snow is easy to find at the pass of Belate, and its own advice then is to abandon the stage or to go on only with extreme caution, along the road from the inn on the climb. This book would add: ask locally before you start, and do not cross on snow you cannot judge. A road in snow has its own risks.
Mud and water.

Eroski notes mud beside the streams on Day 2, a path that turns muddy after a little rain between Enderiz and Olaiz on Day 6, and a stream on the way to Belate that runs with water in the rainy season. Poles or a staff can help on slippery ground; the Xunta says a staff is a great help on stony paths.

spans.t: Roads, gates and traffic

The Policía Foral, the regional police of Navarre, gives the standard advice for walkers on a road: walk on the left, and on the hard shoulder if there is one. In a group, walk in single file. At night or in poor visibility, use lights or reflective clothing.

Visit Navarra says this road keeps away from road traffic. Eroski's descriptions still mention crossings of main roads: beside the frontier at Dantxarinea, below the pass of Otsondo, and on the climb to Belate. Cross with care, and not where a bend hides the traffic. You will also pass field gates and cattle grids. Close gates behind you, and leave the fields as you found them.
Heat and sun

This is not a hot road, but the summer sun is real, and the last day comes down into the Pamplona basin, where Meteo Navarra says July and August maxima average ~28 to ~30 °C. The Xunta advises a cap, high-protection sunscreen, and a water bottle you refill often. Meteo Navarra adds one thing worth knowing for the northern valleys: a south wind can bring a sharp rise in temperature, with warm, dry air that spreads fires quickly. If a fire warning is out, take it seriously, and ask locally.
Your belongings

The Policía Foral's advice for pilgrims is simple: keep your things in sight, carry bags and rucksacks closed and fastened, take only the money you need, in an inner wallet, and keep your passport or identity card somewhere safe. If something is stolen, do not confront the thief; report it to the Policía Foral.
When to stop, and 112

Know your own limits and respect them. If you feel unwell, if a pain grows, or if the weather turns on a hard day, stopping is the right plan, not a failure. For anything that worries you, see a doctor.
112 is the European emergency number
, and it works in France and in Spain. In the mountains, tell your host where you are going and when you expect to arrive.

People walk this road for many reasons, and they do not have to be yours. Some walk out of faith: the road is old, and its oldest buildings are places of welcome for pilgrims. Some walk for sport, or for a rest from work, or to find the French Way from the north, or because they wanted a quiet week among green hills. Some walk out of grief, or at a turning point. Some are curious about a valley they have only seen on a map. All are welcome on the road, and none needs to defend the reason.
A road made of welcome

Visit Navarra names the pilgrims' hospitals and monasteries of Urdax and Belate as the road's notable places, and says they date from the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Eroski Consumer reports a letter of 1378 from the bishop of Bayonne saying that without the hospitality of the hospital at Belate, countless men would be lost in these mountains in winter. You will not need rescuing, but being welcomed in a small village may be something you did not know you needed.

The road also exists today because a few people cared. Eroski says an association of friends of the Camino began in 2000 to recover it, and a pilgrim-hostel directory says that volunteers cleared old paths and rebuilt a chapel stone by stone. You can thank them by walking well, and by leaving the places as you found them.
A frontier on foot

On Day 2 you walk out of one country and into another with no ceremony: Eroski says you pass the old customs buildings and a small stream, the Lapitxuri, as you enter Spain. It may be worth stopping there for a minute.
Pamplona, and a soldier

Pamplona is also where a famous life turned. Wikipedia says that at the Battle of Pamplona, on 20 May 1521, a cannonball that ricocheted off a wall fractured the right leg of a young soldier, Íñigo de Loyola, and that during his recovery he underwent a spiritual conversion. He became Ignatius of Loyola. No source read for this book says he walked this road, and this book does not say so. But if your walk ends in Pamplona, you finish in a city where a soldier's plans ended and another life began.
Walking with a question
You do not need a question, but if you have one it will keep you company. Here is one for each day, to take or leave.

items.t: Bayonne to Ustaritz.
What did you pack because you thought you might need it, and could you leave it behind?
Ustaritz to Urdazubi/Urdax.
You cross a frontier on foot today. What are you leaving on this side?
Urdazubi/Urdax to Elizondo.
The climb comes first. What is the first hard thing you do each day, and how do you begin it?
Elizondo to Berroeta.
An easy short day, with nobody expecting anything of you. What would you do with an open afternoon?
Berroeta to Olagüe.
In the mist you can see only the next few steps. What helps you when you cannot see far ahead?
Olagüe to Pamplona.
Your road meets a bigger one today. Where does your own road meet another, and who will you meet on it?

spans.t: For every kind of walker

If you walk with faith, the little chapel of Santiago at Belate is a place for quiet. If you do not, it is quiet anyway. If your reason is grief, the valley and the rain will ask nothing of you. If you walk to get fit, let the green in anyway. The road does not ask for a reason at the door.
The last streets

After the bridge of the Trinity at Arre you are on the French Way. Eroski Consumer describes the last ~5 km: straight on through Villava and Burlada, over the Magdalena bridge across the river Arga, and into the old city by the Portal de Francia, which the guide to the French Way in this series calls the gate pilgrims from France entered by. The tourist office of Bayonne says you can join the French Way at Pamplona by following the Baztán road from Bayonne, and that is what you have done.

Visit Navarra says the old town has kept its medieval layout. It was formed by three burghs, the Navarrería, San Cernin and San Nicolás, which were united in 1423, when King Charles III the Noble issued the Privilege of the Union. The cathedral of Santa María has, says Visit Navarra, an austere neoclassical façade that hides a Gothic interior: the alabaster tomb of Charles III and his wife Eleanor, the choir stalls, and a Gothic cloister that the page calls one of the best of Europe in its style. Wikipedia dates the Gothic church to the fifteenth century and the façade to 1783. Times for visits change, so ask. Visit Navarra also points to the city walls, which you can walk, and the Renaissance citadel.
In July the city belongs to the festival. Wikipedia says San Fermín runs from noon on 6 July to midnight on 14 July. If you will arrive then, book your bed well in advance.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.
This road ends at Pamplona, and Santiago is far beyond.

The guide to the French Way in this series counts ~712 km and 30 walking days from Pamplona to Santiago, and says other tables differ by several kilometres. The Baztán road, ~109 km, cannot on its own bring you to a Compostela, because the Office's rule counts the last stretch into the cathedral. The Office's pages read for this book do not list the routes it recognises and do not mention the Camino Baztanés. If you plan to carry on to Santiago, and want to know how the Office would read a credencial that begins in Bayonne, ask it before you go. This book does not say whether any start counts.
If you carry on

The French Way continues from Pamplona, and the guide to it in this series is written for that walk. Together, the Baztán road and the French Way from Pamplona make about 820 km, a figure worked out from two estimates, so treat it as a rough guide. Make sure your credencial has room for more stamps.
If you stay

Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. Visit Navarra says a day is hardly enough for Pamplona. Rest. Walk the walls. Sit in a square. Plan your way home with the timetables in front of you, not at the last minute.
The road after the road

A walk of six days is short enough that you may arrive home before it has finished with you. The feet recover in a day or two. The rest takes longer: the green, the quiet, the bridge where your road met another.
Write something down in the first week, while the details are still sharp. A line a day is enough. Keep the credencial, too. It is a record of a road you walked, with its stamps, and it is yours.
Getting home

Plan your way back from Pamplona before you leave it. This book names no timetables, because they change, and no page read for it gives a current one. Look at the times with the evening in front of you, ask your hostel or the tourist office, and do not plan a train or a flight for the afternoon of your last walking day. If you have a spare day, spend it in the city.
Walking again

Eroski Consumer says three Jacobean roads leave from Bayonne: one toward Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, one toward Irun and the coast, and the one you have just walked, to Pamplona. You can walk the others another year. You can also pick up the French Way where this road meets it, and walk on to Santiago in pieces, a week at a time. The guide to the French Way in this series is written for that walk.
Whatever you do next, thank the people who kept the road open for you: the friends of the Camino who cleared the paths, the hosts, the villagers who said
Buen Camino
as you passed.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. It lists the Camino Baztanes as a route from Bayonne to Pamplona, with no stage pages for it yet, so look in it for what is available today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures, bus times and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the stamps the Pilgrim's Office asks for are those on a credencial it recognises. A passport in CaminoPlus is a keepsake.
The Library holds two other books for walkers of this road: a guide to the French Way, which it joins, and
The Pilgrim's Tale
, seven days with the autobiography of Ignatius of Loyola, made to go with the Camino Baztanes.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: Visit Navarra
, the official tourism website of Navarre: the route page, its blog on the road and its six stages, the pages on the Baztán valley, Pamplona and the French Way, and a leaflet of the Policía Foral.
Meteo Navarra
, the regional weather and climate service: the climate of the Atlantic and Middle zones.
The Amis du chemin de St-Jacques Pyrénées-Atlantiques
, the French association: its topo for the voie du Baztan and its route descriptions.
The tourist office of Bayonne
Tourisme 64
and
the commune of Ainhoa
: Bayonne's cathedral and its place among the ways, and Ainhoa.
Eroski Consumer
, a Spanish consumer guide to the Camino: the stage descriptions. Its English pages are machine-translated, so the Spanish originals were read for the figures wherever they loaded.
Albergues del Camino
, a Spanish pilgrim-hostel directory: a second set of stages and the account of the road's recovery. It is a secondary source and is named where used.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
: the rules of the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.
The Xunta de Galicia
and
the Confraternity of St James
: general advice for pilgrims, and a pilgrim passport.
Wikipedia
, English and French: the Voie du Baztan, Baztan, the cathedral of Pamplona, the San Fermín festival and Ignatius of Loyola.
A standard solar calculation
, for sunrise and sunset in Elizondo, and
the CaminoPlus route catalogue
, for the road's name, ends and difficulty rating. The catalogue gives no length and no stage count.

spans.t: Published lengths and heights differ, sometimes by a few kilometres or a few dozen metres, and this book says so. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep this road open: the associations of friends of the Camino on both sides of the frontier, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages who say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Col
or
puerto
: a mountain pass, in French or Spanish.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Policía Foral
: the regional police of Navarre.
Rompepiernas
: "leg-breaker", a hilly stretch.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Voie du Baztan
: the French name of this road.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
